Golden Ticket 001 — a guided SOC investigation
  1 / 1
Start●

You have been handed an alert. Work out what happened.

no experience needed

This is the alert your security team woke up to. Read it before you touch anything:

The alertPossible forged Kerberos tickets - a burst of service-ticket requests from one workstation (10.0.4.10) for many different service names, then domain Administrator logons on servers that workstation has never touched.

Your job is to decide one thing: is this a real attack that must be escalated, or a false alarm that can be closed? You will answer it the way a real analyst does — not by guessing, but by following the evidence from the very first search to the last and writing down what you find as you go. By the final card you will know who broke in, how, to which machines, and when.

What this guide is

Prep1

The words you need to know

read once

You will see all of these in the tool and in your report. Read them once now and the rest of the lab becomes much easier.

The attack

Active DirectoryThe system that holds all the accounts, the servers and the rules about who may touch what, in a Windows organisation. It is the thing being attacked here.
KerberosThe protocol Windows uses to prove identity in an AD network. It works by handing out tickets instead of checking a password at every door.
TGTThe Ticket Granting Ticket — your proof of identity, held by your own machine.
Service ticketA signed slip for one particular service, handed out on request.
SPNService Principal Name — the name of one service, written like CIFS/srv-file-01.corp.local. The first part says what kind of access, the second says which machine. Its field is service.name.
Event 4769The Windows record written every time a service ticket is requested. In a real AD network this is one of the most common records there is, so 4769 by itself means nothing. A burst from one machine means a great deal.
krbtgtA special built-in account whose secret key signs every TGT in the domain. The domain's own ticket-signing key.
Golden ticketA forged TGT. An attacker who has extracted the krbtgt key can mint a TGT for any user, with any groups, with any expiry. No password, no MFA prompt, no failed logon — the forged ticket simply is valid. That is the attack in this lab.

The tool

AlertA rule that fires when something looks dangerous. It is a hint, not a fact. It might be nothing at all.
ElasticsearchThe database that stores and searches the logs. Answers web addresses like localhost:9200.
KibanaThe website you do all the work in, sitting on top of Elasticsearch. Lives at localhost:5601.
IndexOne named pile of log records of the same shape. Ours are auth-* and network-*.
Data viewKibana’s word for “which pile shall I look at”. Older versions called it an index pattern.
DiscoverThe Kibana screen where you type a search and read the matching log lines. You will spend all your time here.
DocumentOne single log record. There are 284 in the auth pile and 136 in network. This is what you read.
FieldOne labelled box inside a document, like service.name. The part before the dot is the group.
KQLThe query language you type into Kibana’s search bar. field: value means “field equals value”, and and joins two conditions.
IOCIndicator of Compromise — a piece of evidence that something bad happened, e.g. an IP address, an account or a file name.
True positiveThe attack is real. Escalate it, contain it, tell someone.
False positiveNothing bad happened. Close the alert with a note saying why not.

The three fields that matter most

Almost every question in this investigation is answered by three fields. Learn these and the whole lab is just typing:

  • event.code — the number of the Windows log record. It tells you what kind of thing happened. You only need three of them:
    4769 = a service ticket was requested  ·  4624 = an account was successfully logged on  ·  4625 = a logon failed
  • source.ip — the address the record came from. On a 4769 it is the machine that asked for the ticket; on a 4624 it is the machine the session arrived from. Your pivot field.
  • service.name — on a 4769, the SPN that was asked for. Comparing its values tells you how wide the attacker was sweeping.
The shape of the attack, before you see it

A golden-ticket attack always has the same four beats: one machine asks for a ticket for a lot of different services in a very short time, those tickets are drawn for an administrative identity, that identity then gets sessions on machines it has never touched, and it reads something. Hold that pattern in your head. By the middle of this lab you will be hunting for it.

The one thing that stops most people

Docker must be installed and running. The lab runs both programs inside Docker containers. If the setup file says docker was not found, or that it is installed but not running, start it — Docker Desktop on Windows or macOS, Docker Engine on Linux — wait until it says it is running, then run the file again. What you should see

A black window that works through numbered stages. It verifies its own work as it goes, so the last thing it prints before the addresses looks like this:

The end of the setup file's own verification query 1 event.code: 4769 = 67 query 2 the ticket burst = 30 query 3 the forged sessions = 3 query 4 the workstation's whole day = 4 query 5 the smb file read = 1 [verify] every number the walkthrough quotes matches the live index.

Those five numbers are the answers to this whole investigation. The script has already proved them against the live index, which is why you can trust every count in the rest of this guide. Then it prints:

The last thing the setup file prints The lab is ready. Elasticsearch : http://127.0.0.1:9200 Kibana : http://127.0.0.1:5601 data view "auth" index pattern auth-* data view "network" index pattern network-*

What it did for you while you waited

So the output does not frighten you, the script performed exactly the jobs that would otherwise be the hard part of this lab:

  • Started two programs — Elasticsearch (the database) and Kibana (the website).
  • Taught Elasticsearch what each field means. An index template declares “event.code holds a number” and “source.ip holds a network address” before any data arrives. Without it Elasticsearch guesses, and guessing quietly breaks your searches.
  • Loaded the log data. If it had already loaded it, it says so and imports nothing — your data cannot load twice.
  • Created your two data views and then read them back to prove the index pattern really was stored. A data view with an empty pattern matches nothing at all, and the cause of that is invisible, so the script checks it instead of hoping.
  • Installed the detection rule and waited for it to fire. The alert you are about to read did not exist until the script did that, and the script does not print ready until the alerts are really there — 30 of them. If the rule had matched nothing, you would have been told so instead of being handed an empty page.

What you are looking at

What one alert says

Two different times, and the difference matters

The alert’s own timestamp is when the rule ran — a minute or two ago, because the rule is still running every minute. The log record underneath it happened on 22 September at 21:45 UTC, which is the night of the attack. So the alerts are new and the events they point at are old, and the alerts page will keep showing them while Discover, which looks at the events themselves, shows you nothing at all until you set its time range. That is the next card, and it is not a fault.

You are not imagining it, and nothing has gone wrong. Open one alert on the JSON tab and you will find two clocks on it:

The two timestamps, from one alert@timestamp 2026-09-29T06:24:19.481Z the day YOU ran this kibana.alert.original_time 2026-09-22T21:45:00.000Z the night of the attack

@timestamp is when Elastic noticed. It is the day you ran the setup file, so it is a different date for every batch and it tells you nothing about the attack. kibana.alert.original_time is when the activity actually happened, and that one never moves — for this lab it is always 22 September. So: an alert is a claim that something happened; the original time is the evidence for it. Every real SOC works this way, because logs often arrive late or a rule is run against history, and if alerts were dated by the event, today’s real alerts would be buried under a wall of old ones.

Which one goes in your report? The original time. Every time you write in this lab, write the time of the activity, never the time the tool noticed it.

The rule that fired

Worth seeing, because the rule and your own investigation are the same filter.

  1. Open the hamburger menu (☰) in the top left, then Security → Rules. That is the page of detection rules; ours is the only one you have, so it sits under Custom rules. Older builds call the page Detection rules.
  2. Find the rule called Burst of Kerberos service-ticket requests from a single workstation.
  3. Read its query. It is event.code: 4769 and source.ip: "10.0.4.10" — character for character the second query in this guide.
Why this is worth two minutes

Because it means the alert count and your query count have to agree. The rule says 30, so when query 2 later returns 30 you have not merely found the same answer twice — you have found the same answer the monitoring system found, by a different road. If the two numbers ever disagree, one of them is wrong, and now you know which one to trust.

no typing needed

You have read the alert. Now come to Discover, where the investigation happens — click the hamburger menu (☰) in the top left and then Discover. This card exists because this screen looks broken, and it is not — the attack is a week old and Discover is looking at the last few minutes, so it is simply showing you nothing yet. Here is the real screen, exactly as you are looking at it now:

Do not click “Try ES|QL” — here is what happens if you do

This build of Kibana includes ES|QL, a different query language, and the Try ES|QL button is an advert for it aimed at people who already know their way around. If you click it you will land on a screen showing this:

The error you will seeFROM logs-*-*,logs-*,filebeat-* | WHERE @timestamp >= ?_tstart AND @timestamp <= ?_tend | LIMIT 10 Unknown index [logs-*-*,logs-*,filebeat-*]

That query looks for indices called logs-* and filebeat-*. Our lab has no such indices — it has auth-* and network-*. So the query cannot work and that error is expected. It does not mean the lab is broken, and there is nothing for you to fix.

What to do instead: press the browser’s Back button to return to the screen above, then carry on. This guide only ever uses the KQL search bar.

So what is wrong right now?

Exactly one thing: the time range. The data view is fine, the search bar is fine, Kibana is healthy. The logs are simply older than the last fifteen minutes.

That is the single most common reason a beginner meets an empty screen. The Search entire time range button fixes it for you. The next card shows you how to do the same thing by hand, so you can pin an exact window rather than “everything”.

Pick a pile5

Choose which pile of logs to look at

which logs?2 min

First, tell Discover which pile of logs to read. You have two, and only one of them is where this attack starts.

Do this

  1. Click the dropdown on the far left of the search bar — the control with the label Data view beside it. It reads auth-*.
  2. Look at the list that opens. There are only two entries that are yours, and this is what it looks like:
The two entries that matter, and what is in them
Data viewDocumentsHolds
auth-*284Logons, Kerberos ticket requests, logoffs, lockouts, privilege assignments, program starts
network-*136Connections between machines: SMB, RPC, DNS, LDAP, HTTP, SSH, ICMP

The * is a wildcard meaning “anything starting with auth”, so a single entry covers every day of auth logs. If you ever see a third entry here that you do not recognise, leave it alone and pick auth-*.

You will still see no documents after closing this panel. That is correct — the time range is still the last 15 minutes. The next card fixes that.

Why this matters

A data view is a bookmark. It tells Kibana which pile of documents to read and which field holds the time. Pick the wrong one and a perfectly good query returns nothing at all, because the documents it is looking for are not in that pile.

So whenever a query returns zero results, check these three things in this order: the data view, then the time range, then the query itself. Nine times out of ten it is one of the first two, never the third.

If the sidebar says “no available fields” and stays that way

Then the data views were not created properly. Do not fight it — run the setup file again. It is safe to run twice, it reloads nothing, and it verifies each data view and tells you if anything is wrong instead of printing a hopeful message.

The one thing that will look “wrong”: Kibana prints times in your timezone

Every timestamp in this lab is stored in UTC, and every picture in this guide was taken on a computer set to UTC. But the @timestamp column, the histogram axis and the friendly dates inside a document all follow your own computer’s timezone, and no setting inside Kibana changes that. If your machine is 8 hours ahead of UTC, the first ticket request that this guide calls Sep 22, 2026 @ 21:45:00.000 will appear in your table as Sep 23, 2026 @ 05:45:00.000.

So which is right? Both, and it does not matter. Here is the rule that keeps you out of trouble:

  • Read the clock times off your own screen and write down what you see. Your timeline will be internally consistent, which is all a timeline needs.
  • Trust the gaps, not the absolute numbers. Every conclusion in this guide is about how far apart things are, and a timezone shift moves every time by the same amount. The gaps — 5 minutes, then 7, then 2, 2, 4 — are identical in every timezone on earth.
  • The gaps are the evidence. The burst is 58 seconds long. The three sessions are 2 minutes apart, then 2. The file read is 4 minutes after the last session. Write those down and you are right in any timezone.

Here is the one table you need if you want to convert a time this guide quotes. Find your own offset, then add or subtract it:

Your computer isExample citiesThen 21:45:00 UTC shows as
UTC+0Lagos, London in winterSep 22 @ 21:45:00
UTC+1Berlin, Paris, MadridSep 22 @ 22:45:00
UTC+2Cairo, Helsinki, JohannesburgSep 22 @ 23:45:00
UTC+5:30India, ColomboSep 23 @ 03:15:00
UTC+8Singapore, Beijing, Perth, Kuala LumpurSep 23 @ 05:45:00
UTC+9Tokyo, SeoulSep 23 @ 06:45:00
UTC−5New York, TorontoSep 22 @ 16:45:00
UTC−6Chicago, Mexico CitySep 22 @ 15:45:00
UTC−8Los Angeles, VancouverSep 22 @ 13:45:00

Not sure what your offset is? Look at the first bar of your histogram and compare it with the 00:00 printed under the left edge. Whatever the difference is, that is your offset. Or simply set your computer’s timezone to UTC before you start — then every picture in this guide matches your screen exactly. Not required. But it removes a whole category of confusion.

What you should have now — the whole lab opens up
  • The Documents tab reads Documents (284).
  • The blue histogram appears with a low line of bars across the day and one tall bar at 21:00. That is your instant visual proof you are looking at the right day.
  • The sidebar lists 19 available fields with a coloured letter beside each one — k for keyword, # for number, t for text, a calendar for dates, and a red box for IP addresses. Those letters tell you what each field can be asked to do.
Remember this one, and it will save you hours

An empty screen in Kibana is almost never a broken query. It is almost always the time range or the data view. Check those two first, every time.

And beware: if you ever press F5 to reload, or wander off to another page and come back, the time range can snap back to Last 15 minutes and the screen goes empty again. That is not your fault and it is not broken — just click Search entire time range again. Some analysts keep the working Discover tab open in a bookmark for exactly this reason.

Investigate7

Query 1 — every service-ticket request that day

1 of 5 queries3 min
Why you are running this query

Before you can say something is unusual, you have to know what normal looks like. 4769 is the record written every time any machine asks for any service ticket, and in a real Active Directory network it is one of the most common records that exist.

So this query deliberately produces a number that tells you nothing. Running it teaches you something worth more than the number: the event code on its own is not a finding.

Do this

Click inside the search bar, select whatever is in it, and paste in exactly this — then press Enter:

Search 1 — type this, then press Enterevent.code: 4769
What 67 actually tells you

67 service tickets were requested across the whole estate that day, and they are smeared evenly from 01:00 to 23:00. There is no burst, no cluster, nothing at any particular moment.

That is exactly what healthy Kerberos traffic looks like: every machine asking for the tickets it needs, all day long, in no particular pattern. If you stop here and write “Kerberos activity looks normal”, you will be right, and you will also have found nothing.

What to do next, and why

You cannot see a shape inside a smear. To find the burst you have to stop counting everybody and start counting one machine at a time — and the alert has already told you which one.

The card after this one, The dead end, proves that 67 really is a dead end by looking at the same records field by field. Then Query 2 narrows to the workstation named in the alert.

Dead end8

Prove the dead end: look at the same 67 field by field

the other tab3 min

Before narrowing to one address, let us be certain that 67 really is a dead end. Kibana has a tool for exactly this question: how is this result set spread out?

Do this

  1. Leave the search bar exactly as it is: event.code: 4769.
  2. Click the Field statistics tab. It is a tab, immediately to the right of Documents (67) — not a section further down the page.
  3. Read three rows: source.ip, user.name and service.name.
The three numbers that close the dead end

Read these off the table and write them down. They are the reason Query 1 cannot answer the question:

RowDistinct valuesWhat it means
source.ip4The 67 requests came from four different machines. No single machine stands out.
host.name4Those same four machines wrote the records.
user.name7Seven different accounts asked for tickets. Seven ordinary people, each asking for what they need.
service.name19Nineteen different services across the whole day, because nineteen different people use nineteen different things.

Four machines, seven users, nineteen services, smeared over twenty-four hours. That is a normal Tuesday. There is nothing here to escalate, and no amount of staring at these 67 records will produce something there is not.

Why a dead end is the most useful card in this lab

Almost every bad alert analysis in the real world dies right here. Somebody queries the scary event code, gets a large number, and then either panics and escalates noise, or shrugs and closes a real incident. Both are mistakes, and both come from stopping at this screen.

You now know what “normal Kerberos” looks like, because you have seen it counted. That is a baseline, and you cannot spot an anomaly without one. Everything from here narrows down to one source address, and every step from here has a small number you can check.

Narrow it9

Query 2 — the burst from the alert’s workstation

2 of 5 queries5 min
Why you are running this query

Four machines, seven users, nineteen services — smeared. Now take one machine out of the mixture. The alert named it: 10.0.4.10.

Your hypothesis is a burst: one machine asking for a lot of different services in a very short time. This query either shows you that shape or it does not. There is no third outcome.

Do this — three parts

  1. Replace the contents of the search bar with this, and press Enter:
Search 2 — type this, then press Enterevent.code: 4769 and source.ip: "10.0.4.10"

Clause by clause: event.code: 4769 keeps only ticket requests; source.ip: "10.0.4.10" keeps only the ones from the workstation named in the alert; and means both must be true. Type the quotation marks exactly.

  1. Look at the Documents tab. It should now read Documents (30). And look at the histogram — this time it is one tall bar.
  2. Add three columns so the rows are readable. In the left sidebar, hover a field name until a + appears, and click it for each of these three:
Field to add as a columnWhy
service.namewhich service the ticket was for — this is the sweep
user.namewhose identity the ticket was drawn for
host.namewhich machine wrote the record

When you add one, it moves up into a new Selected fields group at the top of the sidebar. You now have Selected fields 3, and the table has three column headings after @timestamp. Click the same + again to remove a column if you make a mistake.

  1. Sort oldest first. Click the Sort fields 1 button at the right, above the table, then click Old-New in the panel that opens. The arrow beside @timestamp changes to point up and the first row becomes the oldest.
What those 30 rows prove

Read the four columns and you have the technical signature of a forged ticket. Write every one of these down; they are all of your evidence for the rest of the lab.

  • 30 requests. The tab says Documents (30).
  • 58 seconds, end to end. The first row is Sep 22, 2026 @ 21:45:00.000 and the last is Sep 22, 2026 @ 21:45:58.000. Two seconds apart, every time. A machine on a timer, not a person at a keyboard.
  • One identity, for all 30. The user.name column reads Administrator on every single row. Nobody who uses a domain asks for tickets as Administrator; administrators sign in as themselves and then use the tools they are already entitled to.
  • One machine, for all 30. host.name is ws-sec-02 and source.ip is 10.0.4.10. The records are written on the requesting machine, so these two agree — which is exactly how you know the requests really came from there.

And the important negative finding: no human being needs a file share, a web service, a print server and a domain controller in sixty seconds. A script does, because a script is enumerating — asking for everything it can get a ticket for, to see what sticks. That is what you are looking at.

Count it10

How wide was the sweep? Count the distinct service names.

the sweep number3 min

“Many different services” is a phrase, not a number. Numbers go in reports. Let us turn it into one — and this time the tool will do the counting, so you cannot miscount a list of ten.

Do this

  1. Keep the search bar as it is: event.code: 4769 and source.ip: "10.0.4.10".
  2. Click the Field statistics tab again, next to Documents (30).
  3. Scroll to the service.name row and read its Distinct values cell.
The sweep number: 10

Ten distinct service principal names, thirty requests, three for each, inside 58 seconds. Here they are, so you can see what a sweep looks like — and notice the first one, because you will need it on the last query card:

Service principal name (service.name)Kind of accessRequests
CIFS/srv-file-01.corp.localfile share — the file server3
HTTP/sec-win-04.corp.localweb service on a server3
HOST/sec-win-05.corp.localcomputer account3
HTTP/sec-win-06.corp.localweb service on a server3
LDAP/dc01.corp.localdirectory service — the domain controller3
CIFS/sec-win-04.corp.localfile share on a server3
HOST/sec-win-06.corp.localcomputer account3
HTTP/dc01.corp.localweb service on the domain controller3
CIFS/sec-win-05.corp.localfile share on a server3
HOST/dc01.corp.localcomputer account on the domain controller3

The pattern is mechanical and it is the signature of an enumeration: CIFS, HTTP, HOST, LDAP, CIFS, HOST, HTTP, HTTP, CIFS, HOST — the three commonest service types in a Windows domain, three requests each, in that order, with no repetition of a service already tried. A person who needs a file share asks for the file share. This asked for all three kinds, across four different machines, including the domain controller itself, in under a minute.

Write this down: 30 requests, 10 distinct SPNs, 3 each, 58 seconds, all for Administrator, all from 10.0.4.10.

Why this number is the difference between noise and an incident

In the Query 1 dead end, service.name had 19 distinct values — more than here! And that was normal. So the count of service names on its own proves nothing.

What makes it evidence is the combination: the same account, from the same address, in the same 58 seconds, three times each, for a service it had never asked for before. Any one of these facts is unremarkable. All four together is a forged ticket. That is the habit this lab is trying to build — never trust a single number, look at the shape of the whole record set.

Get the detail11

Open one record and read every field in it

the right button3 min

The table shows you a summary. For the exact values — and for the one field the summary does not show at all — you need to open a record.

Never click the row. Click the little arrow.

Each row has a small button with two arrows pointing diagonally away from each other, in a narrow column immediately to the left of the @timestamp column. Click that. Clicking anywhere else in the row does nothing at all — this is the single most common stumble in this lab, and it makes people think the lab is broken.

Do this

  1. Find the first row — the oldest request, at 21:45:00.000.
  2. Click the ⇉ two-diagonal-arrows button at the far left of that row.
  3. A panel titled Document slides in from the right. Read the message row at the bottom — it is a full English sentence about what this record means, and it is the field the table summary hides.
What this one record says, field by field
FieldValue on this recordWhat it tells you
event.code4,769It is a service-ticket request. (Kibana prints it with a thousands separator; the real value is 4769.)
event.actionkerberos_service_ticket_requestedThe same fact, in words.
event.outcomesuccessThe domain controller issued the ticket. Nothing failed, nothing was denied, no password was guessed.
user.nameAdministratorThe ticket was drawn for the domain administrator identity.
user.domainCORPYour domain.
service.nameCIFS/srv-file-01.corp.localA ticket for the file server. Remember this name — the last query card comes back to it.
source.ip10.0.4.10Where the request came from.
host.ip10.0.4.10The record was written on the same machine, so this really is the requester.
host.namews-sec-02The workstation’s name.
messageA Kerberos service ticket was requested. Account: Administrator. Service Name: CIFS/srv-file-01.corp.local. Source Network Address: 10.0.4.10. Ticket Encryption Type: 0x17. Status: 0x0.The whole record in one sentence. Status: 0x0 means success.

Three things to take from this. First, every single field says the request succeeded — that is what a forged ticket looks like from the domain’s point of view, because to the domain controller the ticket is genuine. Second, no password was involved and nothing failed, so there is no failed-logon trail to find later. Third, a CIFS ticket for the file server was the very first thing this attacker asked for, at 21:45:00, the first row of the burst.

Getting back to the table

Click Close at the bottom of the panel, or the × at its top right, or just press Escape. Your columns and your sort order stay exactly as they were.

Narrow it12

Query 3 — where that identity actually got in

3 of 5 queries4 min
Why you are running this query

You have proved the attacker could get tickets. Tickets are only half a story. What matters is whether those tickets did anything.

This query looks for the moment a ticket was actually used: a successful logon (4624) for the same identity, from the same address. Every machine it succeeds on is now a machine the attacker held domain-admin rights on.

Do this

Replace the contents of the search bar with this — all three clauses matter — and press Enter:

Search 3 — type this, then press Enterevent.code: 4624 and user.name: "Administrator" and source.ip: "10.0.4.10"

event.code: 4624 keeps only successful logons — a different code from Query 2, because those were ticket requests and these are real sessions. user.name: "Administrator" keeps only the domain administrator. source.ip: "10.0.4.10" keeps only the same workstation. You need both halves of the story, so keep all three.

The Documents tab should now read Documents (3). If it reads anything else, you have mistyped a clause — go back and compare character by character.

Three sessions, three servers — this is the scope of the incident

Write this table into your report now. It is the heart of the case.

Time (UTC)AccountServer (host.name)Its addressLogon type
21:52:00.000Administratorsec-win-0410.0.4.203 (network)
21:54:00.000Administratorsec-win-0510.0.4.213 (network)
21:56:00.000Administratorsec-win-0610.0.4.303 (network)

Three things to notice, and all three matter:

  • Three different servers, exactly two minutes apart. That is a machine working through a list, not a person logging in to places they know.
  • Every one is logon.type: 3, a network logon. Nobody was sitting at those machines. Open one of these records and the message field ends with the sentence “Administrative logon; no prior logon from this source to this host.” The log itself is telling you there was no history here.
  • All of them come after the burst, and none during it. Tickets first, then sessions. That order is the attack, and it is the single strongest piece of evidence in this lab. You cannot claim these sessions were forged unless the ticket requests came first — and they did, by seven minutes.
A trap, and it is built into this query on purpose

If you drop the event.code: 4624 clause and search on the account name and the address alone, you get 33 rows, not 3. Try it if you like — then undo it.

Those extra 30 rows are the ticket requests from Query 2, because those were also drawn for Administrator. The event code is the only thing that separates “asked for a ticket” from “got a session”. If you lose it you will report 33 sessions, be wrong, and not know why.

Prove it13

Query 4 — everything that workstation did all day

4 of 5 queries4 min
Why you are running this query

Right now you have three unexplained administrator logons. There is a perfectly innocent explanation available: an administrator was busy tonight.

This query removes that explanation. Drop the account filter and look at everything this one workstation did that day. If those three sessions are all the administrative history it has, they were not routine.

Do this

Replace the contents of the search bar with this — note that user.name is gone, on purpose — and press Enter:

Search 4 — type this, then press Enterevent.code: 4624 and source.ip: "10.0.4.10"

Keep the user.name and host.name columns. Make sure the sort is still Old-New, because the order of these four rows is the finding.

The Documents tab should now read Documents (4). Four. That is the entire day.

“No prior baseline” — the phrase that closes the case

Four rows. That is the whole administrative history of 10.0.4.10 for 22 September 2026. Read it as a story:

  • 21:40 — svc_backup on sec-win-01. An ordinary service account, logging in to a server it has a routine relationship with. Open that record and its message ends “Routine backup service logon.” This is the baseline: this is what this workstation legitimately does, and it gives you something to measure against.
  • 21:52, 21:54, 21:56 — Administrator on sec-win-04, -05 and -06. Three administrative sessions, four minutes end to end, all at the tail of the day.
  • And nothing else. All day. There is no history of this workstation administering those servers at any other time, from any other account. Not once.

That is what “no prior baseline” means, and on its own it is disqualifying. Real administrators log in to the same servers repeatedly, from their own workstation, spread over months. A machine whose entire administrative history fits inside four minutes, on three servers it has never touched, is a machine that was stolen rather than a machine that was used.

Why this one query is worth more than the other three

Queries 1 to 3 gave you counts. This one gives you an absence, and absences are what investigators actually argue from. The three sessions are not suspicious because there were three of them — administrators log in to three servers all the time. They are suspicious because there is nothing else.

It is also the query that separates this alert from a false positive. In a false positive you would find the same administrator on the same servers earlier in the day, from their own machine, repeatedly. You found none of that.

The impact14

Query 5 — switch piles, and find the file read

5 of 5 querieschange data view
Why you are running this query

You have proven capability: the attacker could forge tickets and hold admin sessions on three servers. That is serious, but on its own it is still “nothing was actually taken”.

This query looks for intent and impact. And it has to be run against the other data view, because connections are not authentication events — they are in network-*.

Do this

  1. Click the Data view dropdown on the far left and choose network-*. Watch the sidebar: it now says Available fields 22 instead of 19, because this pile has three extra fields for the far end of a connection.
  2. Your service.name and user.name columns will disappear on their own — those fields do not exist here. That is normal, not an error.
  3. Replace the contents of the search bar with this and press Enter:
Search 5 — type this, then press Enternetwork.protocol: "smb" and source.ip: "10.0.4.10"

network.protocol: "smb" keeps only SMB, which is Windows file sharing and always uses port 445. source.ip: "10.0.4.10" keeps only connections originating from that same workstation.

  1. Add three more columns from the sidebar, the same way as before: destination.ip, destination.port and network.bytes.
One connection, and it is the whole impact
  • Exactly one SMB session from 10.0.4.10 all day. Not several. One.
  • To 10.0.4.12 on port 445. That is the file server. Note it is not one of the three servers from Query 3 — the attacker read a fourth machine, and did it over the network rather than through a logon record.
  • 262,144 bytes, which Kibana prints as 262,144. That is exactly 256 KB — a suspiciously round number, and far too much to be incidental. Write the byte count down.
  • At 22:00:00.000, four minutes after the last forged session and fifteen minutes after the ticket burst.

This is what turns a serious alert into a reportable breach. Ticket activity proves capability; an actual 256 KB data transfer proves intent and gives you the scope you need for the notification and legal side of the response.

Close it15

Read the file record, and close the loop

the smoking gun

One more click and the case is complete. Open the SMB record and read its message field.

Do this

  1. Click the ⇉ two-diagonal-arrows button on the left of the single row. Not the row — the button.
  2. Scroll the Document panel down to the message field and read it in full.
The message field, in full
The whole sentence, exactly as the log records itSMB session from 10.0.4.10 (ws-sec-02) to 10.0.4.12:445 (srv-file-01), authenticated as CORP\Administrator. 262144 bytes read in one session.

Four facts in one sentence, and every one of them is new:

  • The file server has a name: srv-file-01. Until now you only had its address, 10.0.4.12.
  • It was authenticated as CORP\Administrator — the same forged identity from Query 3, on a machine you had not seen it log on to.
  • 262,144 bytes read in one session. The read completed in a single connection, which is what you expect when a tool is pulling a known file rather than a person browsing.
  • It came from ws-sec-02 at 22:00:00.000 — the attacker’s own workstation, fifteen minutes after the ticket burst.
Now close the loop — this is the part that makes the report good

Go back to your Query 2 results. The very first row of the burst, the one you opened ten cards ago, was a request for:

The first service name in the burst — the same file serverCIFS/srv-file-01.corp.local

That is the same machine. CIFS means file share, and srv-file-01 is the name the log just gave you.

So the complete chain reads: at 21:45:00 the attacker asked for a ticket to the file server → over the next 58 seconds it asked for nine other services too → at 21:52, 21:54 and 21:56 it used the forged identity to get into three other servers → at 22:00 it went back to the file server it had named first and read 256 KB.

It requested the ticket for the thing it was actually going to steal, in the very first second of the burst. That is not opportunistic. That is a plan, and it is the single most persuasive sentence you can put in your report — and notice that the lab never told you to look for it. You found it by reading a field nobody pointed at.

A note on why three of the ten SPNs are not suspicious

Three of the services in the burst — CIFS/srv-file-01, LDAP/dc01 and HOST/dc01 — also appear in the ordinary traffic you saw in Query 1. The reason is the whole lesson of Kerberos detection: you cannot identify this attack by its event code or by its service names. Plenty of legitimate traffic uses those same names.

Only the source address isolates it. Every ordinary ticket request in this data set was written by the machine that made it, and none of them came from 10.0.4.10 except these 30. That is why Query 2 is the query that matters, and why Query 1 was worth running even though it told you nothing.

Put it together16

Build the timeline

most important 5 min

This is the most important 5 minutes in the lab. Investigators do not just collect facts — they arrange them so the facts argue the conclusion for them.

Do this

Open a text file (Notepad is fine) and write six lines, oldest first, copying the times off your own screen. The yellow blank is your work — read it off your table and type it in. The gaps on the right are pre-filled, because gaps are the same in every timezone and they are the actual evidence.

  1. 21:40:00.000  →  fill in from your screen
    The baseline. An ordinary successful logon for svc_backup on sec-win-01 from 10.0.4.10. “Routine backup service logon.” This is the only legitimate thing this workstation did all day.
  2. 21:45:00.000  →  21:45:58.000  (58 seconds)
    The burst. 30 Kerberos service-ticket requests (4769) from 10.0.4.10, 2 seconds apart, for 10 distinct service names, 3 each, all drawn for Administrator. The first one asked for is CIFS/srv-file-01.corp.local.
  3. 21:52:00.000  (+2 min)
    First forged session. Successful logon (4624, logon.type 3) for Administrator on sec-win-04 from 10.0.4.10. The log itself notes “no prior logon from this source to this host.”
  4. 21:54:00.000  (+2 min)
    Second forged session, same account, same source, on sec-win-05.
  5. 21:56:00.000  (+2 min)
    Third forged session, same account, same source, on sec-win-06.
  6. 22:00:00.000  (+4 min)
    The impact. SMB read from 10.0.4.10 to 10.0.4.12:445 — which is srv-file-01, the file server named in the first ticket request — 262,144 bytes, authenticated as CORP\Administrator.

The clock times above are UTC, which is how the lab stores them and how this guide’s pictures were taken. If your screen is showing a different offset, write down your numbers instead — what matters is that the six lines stay in this order and keep these gaps: 5 minutes from the baseline to the burst, then 7 from the burst to the first session, then 2, 2, 4.

The shape of the answer

A quiet baseline logon, then everything else in the lab happens inside 20 minutes, at the very end of the day, in strict order: requests, then sessions, then a file read. Nothing is hours apart, nothing is days apart.

That tightness is itself evidence. It rules out coincidence, and it rules out routine administration.

Then ask the questions that turn facts into a verdict

QuestionYour answer, and the query that proved it
Who started it?source.ip: 10.0.4.10
What did they take?262,144 bytes from srv-file-01 (10.0.4.12)
How did they get in?forged Kerberos tickets — 30 requests, 10 SPNs, 58 seconds, for Administrator
How far did they get?four machines: sec-win-04, -05, -06 and srv-file-01
Why is it not routine?the workstation had no prior administrative history on any of them
The one-sentence verdict

On 22 September 2026 a single workstation, 10.0.4.10, issued a 58-second burst of 30 Kerberos service-ticket requests covering 10 distinct service principal names for the domain Administrator identity, then used that identity to open network logon sessions on three servers it had never previously contacted, and finally read 256 KB from a fourth, srv-file-01, whose CIFS service name was the first one in the burst.

That is a true positive. Every clause of that sentence is traceable to one of the five queries you just ran. That is what a finished investigation looks like.

Your verdict in one line

Two things worth double-checking in your own report

These are the two that catch people out, so read yours back now:

  1. Did you narrow to the source address? A report that stops at “event.code: 4769 returned a lot of rows, and Kerberos looks normal” is incomplete. The event code on its own is not a finding — you had to add a source address before the picture appeared.
  2. Did your session query keep event.code? If you dropped it, the ticket requests you drew earlier get counted as logons too, because they were drawn for the same identity. Check which filter you actually left in before you trust the number.

And one bonus: if you noticed that the file server’s CIFS service name appears in the ticket burst, say so in your report. It is not required, and nothing checks it automatically, but it is the sentence that turns a list of counts into a story.

Finish18

Tear the lab down

one file1 min

One file removes everything the lab created. Nothing is left running, and nothing of yours is deleted.

Do this

  1. Make sure you have submitted your report. The teardown deletes the data.
  2. Close your browser and every Kibana tab.
  3. In the lab folder, run the teardown file for your system: on Windows, double-click teardown.cmd; on macOS or Linux, run ./teardown.sh in a terminal in that folder (or bash teardown.sh).
  4. It prints the exact list of what it is about to remove, and asks you to confirm (Y or N on Windows, y or n on macOS and Linux). Read the list, then say yes.
  5. It finishes by verifying the removal and telling you what was kept.
The list the teardown file prints before it deletes anything The following will be REMOVED. Nothing else will be touched. container golden-ticket-001-elasticsearch container golden-ticket-001-kibana volume golden-ticket-001_esdata (this holds ALL the lab data) file .../golden-ticket-001-/docker-compose.yml folder .../elklab-golden-ticket-001-

Yours will show a different path — a Windows path on Windows, a /var/folders/... or /tmp/ one on a Mac. The five names are the same everywhere, and only the names are ever deleted.

What it will never touch

Every name in that list is derived from the folder name, and nothing else is considered for deletion. In particular:

  • No Docker images are removed. They are large and slow to download, so they are kept and the next setup is fast and works offline.
  • No other container or volume on this machine is touched, so a second lab running beside this one is safe.
  • Your files stay. The log data, the templates and this guide are all still in the folder afterwards.

The teardown file never runs docker system prune and never removes an image. It says so on screen before it starts, and it means it.

If you would rather just stop it and keep the data

Sometimes you want the lab back tomorrow without waiting for it to reload. Stop the containers but keep everything, and start them again later with one command:

Run this in a terminal, in the lab folderdocker compose -f docker-compose.yml down

Your data lives in the Docker volume, so it survives. Bring it all back with docker compose -f docker-compose.yml up -d, or simply run the setup file again — it is safe to run twice and will not re-import anything.

Running teardown twice is harmless

It checks what is actually there first, tells you there is nothing to do, and exits. It will not complain and it will not delete anything else looking for something to clean up. That matters, because people run it twice to be sure.

Reference19

If something goes wrong

not a steplook me up

Three things account for almost every problem in this lab. Work down the list rather than guessing.

1. The screen is empty and there are no documents

Almost never a broken query. Check, in this order:

  1. Is the data view right? It must say auth-* for queries 1 to 4 and network-* for query 5.
  2. Is the time range right? If it says Last 15 minutes, the data is older than that and you will see nothing. Click Search entire time range again. This is by far the most common cause, and it happens after pressing F5 or navigating away and back.
  3. Is the query in the bar at all? It should be in plain text, not in a leftover filter row underneath.
If the Alerts page is the empty one

Same cause, different page. An alert is stamped with the time the rule ran, not the time the event happened, so the alerts page starts on Today and the log data is from September 2026. If the Alerts page is empty, set its time picker to Last 24 hours or 1 day and the thirty come back. The alert card explains the two timestamps, because this one catches everyone out at least once.

2. The counts do not match this guide

You seeWhat it almost certainly means
Double every numberThe data was imported twice. Run the setup file with reset and then it again, which rebuilds the data exactly once.
Nothing for query 5You are still on the auth-* data view. Query 5 has to run on network-*.
33 instead of 3You dropped event.code: 4624 from query 3, so the 30 ticket requests were counted as sessions too.
Times are hours offThat is your timezone, not a fault. Read the gaps, not the absolute clock times — see the time-range card.
Dates in the past, on a computer years aheadExpected, and not a fault. The log data is a real day in September 2026 and never moves. The rule that raises the alerts only looks back a year, so it keeps finding it.
The sidebar says 0 available fieldsStill a time-range problem. Click Search entire time range.

3. The lab will not start

What the setup file saysWhat to do
docker was not foundDocker Desktop is not installed. Ask your instructor.
Docker is installed but the engine is not respondingOpen Docker Desktop and wait until it says Engine running, then run the file again.
something else is already using port 9200Another lab is running. The script refuses to touch it, correctly. Stop the other one, or run teardown.cmd from the folder that owns it.
a container called golden-ticket-001-elasticsearch already existsThe folder was copied or moved, so a previous copy owns the container. The script shows you the details and stops without deleting anything. Follow the two docker commands it prints, or run teardown.cmd from the original folder first.
Elasticsearch did not become ready in timeIt prints the last 40 lines of the container log. Usually not enough memory for Docker; close other applications, or give Docker Desktop more memory in its settings.
the auth index holds N documents but this lab ships 284A partial load. The script refuses to import on top of it, because that would create duplicates. Run setup-lab.cmd reset.

Two controls that catch people out

  • Clicking a table row does nothing. You need the small ⇉ two-diagonal-arrows button immediately to the left of the @timestamp column. In the Document panel, Escape closes it.
  • The Field statistics tab shows one row per FIELD, not one row per value. It will not give you “113 and 104” style counts — for an exact number, run the query and read the Documents tab.
The 30-second checklist

Data view right? → Time range says a date, not “Last 15 minutes”? → Query text in the bar? → Number in the Documents tab matches the number this guide quotes? If all four are true and something still looks wrong, press F5 and re-click Search entire time range, then re-run the queries from the top. If Query 1 does not return a large number of documents, your time range is still wrong; if it does, the problem is in the query text rather than in the dates.
